title: Heritage sites in Ladakh: Alchi, Hemis, Leh Palace and rock art
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Ladakh: Alchi, Monasteries and Rock Art
meta_description: Heritage sites in Ladakh: Alchi's painted temples, Lamayuru, Hemis, Thiksey, Leh Palace, Basgo, the Mulbekh Maitreya and petroglyphs along the Indus.
summary: Ladakh's best known heritage site is Alchi, whose temples of about the 11th to 13th centuries hold some of the finest early Buddhist murals in the Himalaya. Add the monasteries of Lamayuru, Hemis, Thiksey and Likir, Leh Palace and Basgo of the Namgyal kings, rock-carved Maitreya images at Mulbekh, and thousands of petroglyphs along the Indus. Ladakh has no UNESCO site.

paras: Ladakh sits on routes linking Kashmir, Tibet and Central Asia, and its history follows the trade in wool, salt and pashmina that passed through Leh. Rock carvings show people and animals in the region long before Buddhism. From about the 10th century a West Tibetan dynasty ruled, and the second diffusion of Buddhism brought temple building and Kashmiri artists. The Namgyal dynasty ruled from the 16th century until the Dogra conquest in the 1830s.

Most of Ladakh's heritage is still in use: monasteries with resident monks, villages of flat-roofed houses and chortens, and festivals with masked cham dances. Our guide to [Buddhist caves in India](buddhist-caves-in-india.html) gives the earlier Indian background to its art.

Alchi Choskor, on the Indus west of Leh, is a group of small temples built in about the 11th to 13th centuries. Their walls and ceilings are covered in murals painted in a style closely linked to Kashmir, with mandalas, rows of Buddhas, and scenes of court life with figures in rich textiles. The Sumtsek, a three-storey temple, holds large clay images of Bodhisattvas whose painted dhotis are a record of medieval textile design.

Mangyu and Sumda Chun, in side valleys, have temples of the same period. The interiors are fragile and photography inside is usually not allowed. Our lecture [Reading sculpture](reading-sculpture.html) and the session on [temple sculpture and iconography](temple-sculpture-iconography.html) help visitors identify the figures they see.

Lamayuru, on the old road to Kashmir, is one of the oldest monastic sites in Ladakh, set above eroded clay formations. Likir, Thiksey, built on a hill like a small Potala, and Hemis, the wealthiest monastery and site of a large summer festival, are the most visited. Spituk, Phyang and Diskit in Nubra add more.

Leh Palace, built in the 17th century under Sengge Namgyal, rises nine storeys above the old town and has been restored by the ASI. Basgo, an earlier Namgyal seat, keeps a mud-brick citadel and temples with murals. Shey Palace has a large seated Buddha. Our [Leh heritage walk guide](heritage-walk-in-leh.html) covers the old town below the palace.

Petroglyphs are found on boulders along the Indus and its tributaries, at places such as Domkhar, Tangtse and Alchi. They show ibex, yaks, hunters, horse riders and later Buddhist stupas and inscriptions, and span a long period that is hard to date precisely. Our programme [Rock art of India](rock-art-of-india.html) explains how these carvings are recorded.

At Mulbekh, on the road to Kargil, a standing figure of Maitreya about nine metres high is carved in relief on a rock face, probably in the 7th to 8th centuries. Kartse Khar in the Suru valley has a similar carved image, and Apati has another.

sections.h2: Planning a heritage visit to Ladakh
paras: Leh is about 3,500 metres above sea level, so plan two days to acclimatise before any sightseeing. June to September is the main season. Some areas need an Inner Line Permit or Protected Area Permit, depending on route and nationality.
We build a [study tour for your group](a-study-tour-built-for-your-group.html) to Leh, Alchi, Basgo and Lamayuru, with a briefing on Buddhist art beforehand.

faq.q: Are there UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Ladakh?
faq.a: No. Ladakh has no site on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Alchi and other monasteries and landscapes have been discussed for nomination, but none is listed.

Alchi's temples, built in about the 11th to 13th centuries, preserve some of the finest early Buddhist murals in the Himalaya, painted in a style linked to Kashmir. The clay Bodhisattvas in the Sumtsek temple are also famous for their painted textiles.

faq.q: Which are the oldest monasteries in Ladakh?
faq.a: Lamayuru and Alchi are among the oldest monastic sites, with foundations linked to the 10th to 11th centuries. Many of the large hill monasteries such as Hemis and Thiksey date from later centuries.

faq.q: Where can you see rock art in Ladakh?
faq.a: Petroglyphs are found along the Indus and its tributaries, including at Domkhar, Tangtse and near Alchi. They show animals, hunters and later Buddhist motifs, carved over a long period.
